Exercise 8.2 · Week 8

Test the Best Score

Python in Thonny Work in pairs

Goal: write tests that catch bugs hiding at the edges.

best_score(scores) in score_tools.py finds the highest score in a list. It is correct. Your job is to write tests that would catch it if somebody broke it one day.

  1. Read score_tools.py. What should best_score([]) give?
  2. Open starter.py. One normal test is done for you. Press Run: pytest says PASSED for every test. (The empty ones pass too: a test with no assert checks nothing!)
  3. TODO 1 test the empty list. TODO 2 test a list where the best score is the last one. TODO 3 write one more edge-case test.
  4. Press Run again. Every test should say PASSED.

Done looks like: at least 3 tests, all PASSED.

Edge cases to think about: an empty list, one item, the first item, the last item, all the same.

Starter code

Open starter.py in Thonny, or copy the code below into a new file and save it as starter.py.

"""MY TESTS for best_score()  -  this file is YOUR test file.

Read score_tools.py first to see what best_score() should do.
Then write tests for the NORMAL case and for the EDGE cases: the places
where bugs like to hide (empty lists, the first item, the last item...).

Press the green Run button to run your tests with pytest.
"""

from score_tools import best_score


def test_best_score_in_the_middle():
    # Normal case: the best score is in the middle of the list.
    assert best_score([3, 9, 2]) == 9, "9 is the biggest of 3, 9 and 2"


def test_empty_list():
    # TODO 1 (edge case): no games played yet. What should best_score([]) give?
    pass


def test_best_score_at_the_end():
    # TODO 2 (edge case): make a list where the biggest score is the LAST one.
    pass


# TODO 3: one more test of your own. Ideas: a list with only one score,
#         or a list where every score is the same.


if __name__ == "__main__":
    import pytest
    pytest.main(["-v", __file__])
Download starter.py

Stuck? Open a hint

Try on your own first. Hints open one at a time, from a small nudge to a bigger one. None of them gives the answer away.

Hint 1: Where to look

Read the top of score_tools.py. It lists what best_score() gives for a few lists, including an empty one. Your edge-case tests should check these places where a bug could hide.

Hint 2: Try this

A test is only real if it has an assert line. The shape is assert function(input) == expected_answer. Pick a list, work out the answer yourself, and write it after ==. Keep the message text short and clear.

Hint 3: Almost there

Shapes to fill in: assert best_score(____) == ____, "message". For the end test, put the biggest number in the last spot of the list. For your own test, try a list with ____ item, or a list where every number is the same.
